transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-08
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Jonah Li (Redwood SE), Rafa Gomez (Redwood SE), Ellen Park (CTO - DataVista), Mike Johnson (ML Engineer), Priya Verma (VP Product)

Summary: quick product walkthrough focused on structured output / JSON mode and function/tool calling features. Customer cares about predictable output schemas, guardrails for downstream tools, and security (VPC/KMS/SOC2). Asked about hosted vs dedicated performance/cost tradeoffs and how rollouts / canary behave for schema changes.

Topics: structured output, JSON schema enforcement, function calling, tool integrations, guardrails for hallucination, batching/latency tradeoffs, private deployment options (VPC/on-prem), SOC2/KMS, trial POC plan

Transcript:
[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Samira from Redwood, joined by Jonah and Rafa. How are you all doing?
[00:05] Ellen: Doing well, thanks. Excited to see how the structured output stuff can help our payments reconciliation flows.
[00:12] Mike: Hi, quick note, we're trying to replace a brittle regex pipeline that breaks on new vendor formats, so deterministic JSON output would be huge.
[00:20] Jonah: Totally, that's exactly the use case we wanted to show. We'll demo JSON mode, schemas, and then function calling so you can have the model return structured payloads we can directly route to downstream services.
[00:31] Rafa: I'll start by sharing my screen, should be up in a sec. (slight crosstalk) okay, can you see the console?
[00:40] Priya: Yep. The console looks clean-ish. We care about output validation — if schema changes break things how do we detect?
[00:48] Jonah: Good question. We support strict JSON mode where the model is constrained by a provided schema. You get an error or a validation flag when the output doesn't match. Also, Redwood Optimize can monitor regressions against a test set and alert if schema adherence drops.
[01:05] Mike: Is that runtime enforcement or post-hoc? We need something that prevents bad payloads from ever hitting our payment microservices.
[01:12] Samira: You can do both. At request time you can enable strict mode which returns a schema validation failure and an alternate fallback response, or route to a canary path that runs additional verification. We also have pre-commit style checks in the console for rollout policies.
[01:28] Ellen: How deterministic is the structured output? Sometimes models add extra fields or reorder arrays and that messes up our ingestion.
[01:36] Jonah: We showed with JSON mode plus an explicit schema and a short system priming, outputs are highly consistent. There's still a small failure rate depending on prompt variability; that's where auto-retry with stricter sampling and our prefix caching helps. We can show benchmarks in the POC.
[01:53] Priya: On the POC, we'll want to see tail latency at our 512 token typical length. Also cost per node, what's the unit economics between hosted and dedicated?
[02:03] Samira: Hosted is simplest to start and you can get good latency with our optimized kernels; dedicated gives you reserved capacity and better predictable throughput so unit cost often drops at scale. We'll send a cost/latency comparison tailored to your request volume.
[02:18] Mike: We're in GCP. Any issues with region or VPC peering? Data residency is also a thing.
[02:25] Rafa: We support VPC peering and Private deployments. For regulated data you can run Redwood Private in your VPC or on-prem; KMS/HSM integrations are available for key management and logs feed into your SIEM. We'll include our SOC2/ISO pack for your security team.
[02:42] Ellen: Great. Can you dig into function calling? We have a separate service that applies business rules — ideally the model would return a structured call to that service with arguments already normalized.
[02:53] Jonah: Yep. Function calling lets you define a contract — schema for the function name and parameters. In the demo, we'll pass an 'apply_reconciliation' function with fields vendor, amount_cents, invoice_date, and tags. Redwood's tool calling ensures the model's output is parsed into a JSON object and we validate against the function schema before invoking.
[03:14] Mike: If the model hallucinates a field name or returns malformed types, what's the guardrail?
[03:20] Rafa: We surface a structured validation result. You can configure a strict reject, a sanitized mapping, or a human review queue. For sensitive flows we recommend strict validation + canary routing.
[03:32] Priya: Any rate limit or concurrency issues if we batch multiple requests? We expect bursts during end-of-day processing.
[03:39] Jonah: Redwood has workload-aware batching and autoscaling for dedicated pools. For hosted, we recommend rate limits + burst policies; for sustained high throughput, Dedicated gives SLOs for latency and throughput.
[03:52] Ellen: We're also interested in model versioning. If you roll out a new model that subtly changes field formatting, can we pin schema versions?
[04:00] Samira: Absolutely. You can pin model versions per route and tie schema versions to rollouts. We support canary deploys and automatic rollback rules if quality metrics drop under threshold. Redwood Optimize can run A/B evals against your golden prompts.
[04:15] Mike: Is there a way to automatically generate a schema from sample outputs? That would speed up onboarding.
[04:21] Jonah: We have a schema suggestion tool in the console that infers likely schema from example outputs and flags ambiguous fields. It's a starting point but we recommend reviewing before locking to strict mode.
[04:34] Priya: Security: SSO, SAML integration for ops team and RBAC for routes?
[04:39] Rafa: Yes to SAML/SSO, SCIM provisioning, and fine-grained RBAC. Auditing/logs include token-level usage and per-route latency and cost breakdowns.
[04:52] Ellen: Any mention of competitors — we've evaluated OpenAI function calling and Anthropic. Why Redwood?
[04:58] Samira: The big differentiators are production-first tooling: unified runtime across hosted/dedicated/private, built-in rollout and canary controls, and cost-aware knobs (batching, quantization recommendations). We also provide first-class observability for token-level cost which helps ops teams.
[05:16] Mike: Let's do a short live example?
[05:18] Jonah: Sure. I'll show an API snippet that calls JSON mode with a schema. (typing noises) Here is the request: system prompt + schema object, mode: json_strict, schema: {"type":"object","properties":{"vendor":{"type":"string"},"amount_cents":{"type":"integer"},"invoice_date":{"type":"string","format":"date"}},"required":["vendor","amount_cents"]} — note, that's illustrative.
[05:45] Priya: The console also shows the example and a 'validate' button?
[05:49] Rafa: Correct, you can preview sample outputs, run a batch of examples, and the console will show pass/fail and diffs.
[05:58] Mike: In the demo the model returned vendor: 'Acme Co' and amount_cents as string sometimes — how do you coerce types?
[06:05] Jonah: We have type coercion helpers and a validation layer. For strict mode, the request would be marked as failed; with a relaxed policy we can attempt coercion (e.g., parse numeric strings) and report the correction in the response metadata.
[06:19] Ellen: For function calling, we want the function signature to be stable. If we change schema, will previous invocations still map?
[06:26] Samira: You can version function schemas and the console keeps a history. During rollout, you can run the new schema on a shadow route to check mappings before flipping traffic.
[06:36] Priya: Can this tie into our workflow engine? We use Temporal for orchestration.
[06:41] Rafa: Absolutely — function calling returns structured payloads you can send to Temporal. We also provide a small webhook connector if you want event-driven triggers.
[06:51] Mike: Any security concerns with function invocation? We need to ensure the model can't trigger destructive operations.
[06:58] Jonah: We recommend allowing only a whitelisted set of functions, with RBAC on who can add functions. Also sandboxing and pre-invocation validation ensures the payload meets expected constraints.
[07:12] Ellen: Ok, for the POC we'd like: 1) a 2-week benchmark comparing hosted vs Dedicated (latency/cost) 2) a schema strictness test on 1k real invoices 3) security review with our compliance team.
[07:23] Samira: That sounds doable. We'll provision a trial and run the benchmark with you. Jonah will coordinate the test harness.
[07:30] Priya: Pricing — can you give ballpark numbers now?
[07:34] Samira: Ballpark yes: hosted per-token pricing depends on model family, but for your volume we expect Dedicated to be more cost-effective after commit. We'll send a tailored estimate in the follow-up.
[07:45] Mike: One last technical: prefix caching and KV cache — will that help with repeated vendor names?
[07:51] Jonah: Yes, caching reduces repeated compute for shared prefixes. For reconciliation flows where prompts share context, it helps reduce latency and cost significantly.
[07:59] Ellen: Great. Anything else?
[08:02] Rafa: I'll drop links to the schema examples and a short notebook that shows function calling + validation.
[08:08] Samira: Recap: we'll send pricing + SOC2 docs, provision trial, Jonah will set up POC benchmark, Rafa shares slides and schemas.
[08:18] Priya: Thanks everyone, this was useful.
[08:22] Mike: Thanks, bye.
[08:25] Ellen: Bye.

End notes: demo included a short live API example and console walkthrough. Several small transcription artifacts (screen share audio, brief crosstalk).
